issues.legal_issue: A binding decision upholding a constitutional amendment cannot be reopened merely because a later challenge advances new arguments.
material_facts: The constitutional validity of Article 31A had been upheld by a thirteen-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati.
The challenge sought to reopen that ruling through further arguments, but the Court found no basis to displace the binding precedent.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to reconsider Article 31A’s validity and treated the prior ruling as binding.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 141 and the doctrine of stare decisis, the ruling in Kesavananda Bharati upholding Article 31A binds the Court; a decision does not lose authority merely because it is later said to have been badly argued, inadequately considered, or fallaciously reasoned.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_amendment: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of an amendment.
predicates.controlling_larger_bench_upheld_amendmen: A controlling larger bench had upheld the amendment’s validity.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_new_arguments: The challenger seeks reconsideration by advancing arguments against the amendment.

issues.definition: When a constitutional amendment has been upheld by a controlling larger bench, a constitutional challenge based on further arguments is rejected as precluded by binding precedent.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation imposing ceilings on land holdings falls within the protection for agrarian reform legislation.
material_facts: The challenged legislation imposed ceilings on agricultural land holdings and sought to redistribute surplus land and promote rural development.
The Court described equitable land distribution, ending concentrated ownership through ceilings, and rural economic planning as features of agrarian reform.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that Article 31A’s protection extends to land-ceiling legislation against challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A broadly protects agrarian reform, including land-ceiling measures; the Court relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab and State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing (Weaving) Co. Ltd. The Court also stated that it did not rest its ultimate decision on Article 31A.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law that limits land holdings.
predicates.law_redistributes_land: The challenged law is directed toward distributing land more equitably.
predicates.law_limits_concentrated_land_ownership: The challenged law limits concentrated ownership of land through ceilings.

issues.definition: A land-ceiling law challenged constitutionally falls within agrarian-reform protection when it redistributes land or limits concentrated land ownership.

issues.legal_issue: The right to personal liberty does not make a land-reform measure regulating property constitutionally reviewable under the personal-liberty guarantee merely because the measure is alleged to be unreasonable.
material_facts: The challengers argued that deprivation of property under land-reform legislation also impaired personal liberty under the expansive interpretation of Article 21 in Maneka Gandhi.
The legislation concerned land ownership and ceilings, rather than personal liberty.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the Article 21 challenge and held that Maneka Gandhi did not supply a general remedy for challenges to land-reform laws affecting property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished personal liberty under Article 21 from proprietary rights addressed by Articles 19 and 31, and held that Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India was not a universal cure applicable to land-reform legislation.

predicates.land_reform_property_challenge: The proceeding challenges a land-reform measure affecting property.
predicates.alleged_injury_is_property_deprivation: The challenger relies on deprivation or regulation of property as the alleged injury.
predicates.no_personal_liberty_issue_is_shown: The challenger does not show an injury to personal liberty distinct from the property effect.

issues.definition: A property-based challenge to a land-reform measure does not succeed under the personal-liberty guarantee when no distinct personal-liberty injury is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A qualified rule disregarding certain post-cutoff land transfers to prevent evasion of a land ceiling is a reasonable restriction on property rights.
material_facts: The ceiling law directed the authority to disregard certain transfers made after a specified statutory date if, without the transfer, the land would have been declared surplus.
The law preserved exceptions for transfers made in good faith for adequate consideration under an irrevocable instrument and not for the benefit of the transferor or family members.
The Court found that invalidating transfers made after the cutoff served the purpose of preserving surplus land for redistribution and was not a blanket prohibition.
issues.conclusion: The Court held the transfer rule fair and valid, and not violative of the property-right restriction in Article 19(1)(f).
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) was subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6). The legislature could adopt measures ancillary to a land-ceiling policy to prevent transactions defeating that policy; Section 5(6) was upheld as a qualified, purpose-related restriction.

predicates.land_ceiling_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges a restriction operating as part of a land-ceiling law.
predicates.post_cutoff_transfers_could_reduce_surpl: Transfers made after a specified cutoff could leave less land available as surplus.
predicates.transfer_rule_is_qualified_and_purpose_r: The rule disregards only specified transfers and is directed at preventing evasion of the ceiling policy.

issues.definition: A qualified, purpose-related rule preventing post-cutoff transfers from reducing surplus land is valid when challenged as part of a land-ceiling law.

issues.legal_issue: An allowance of additional land to a landholder on account of adult sons does not, without deprivation of women’s property or unequal treatment of women as landholders, establish unconstitutional sex discrimination.
material_facts: The law allowed a landholder additional permissible area on account of adult sons but not adult daughters.
The additional area remained the landholder’s property; the adult son acquired no property right under that allowance.
The law did not take a daughter’s property while retaining a son’s property, or deny a daughter a share given to a son.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no tangible sex discrimination in the additional-area rule and rejected the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 15 do not invalidate a land-ceiling scheme on this ground where it does not discriminate between male and female landholders or take women’s property. The Court held that Section 5(3) did not confer property on an adult son or withdraw property from an adult daughter.

rule.if: sex_discrimination_challenge_to_land_ceiling_law and adult_son_based_allowance and no_child_acquires_property_from_allowance and women_property_is_not_taken

predicates.sex_discrimination_challenge_to_land_cei: The proceeding alleges sex discrimination in a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.adult_son_based_allowance: The scheme allows a landholder additional permissible area because of adult sons.
predicates.no_child_acquires_property_from_allowanc: Neither the adult son nor another child acquires property merely because of the allowance.
predicates.women_property_is_not_taken: The scheme does not take a woman’s property while retaining comparable property belonging to a man.

issues.definition: An adult-son-based allowance does not establish unconstitutional sex discrimination when it gives no child property and does not take women’s property.

issues.legal_issue: Treating a husband as the tenure holder for administrative purposes when his wife owns land does not violate equality guarantees if her ownership and compensation rights are preserved.
material_facts: The law treated the husband as the tenure holder even where the wife owned the land.
The Court found that this treatment simplified dealings and did not affect ownership or enjoyment of land within the permissible limit.
If the wife’s land was taken as surplus, compensation was payable to her, and the law protected her in selecting land to be declared surplus.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the tenure-holder definition was not discriminatory and rejected the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 15 do not invalidate a procedural device that treats the husband as tenure holder where it does not diminish the wife’s ownership or rights to compensation. The Court relied on Sections 3(17) and 12A and the compensation provisions in Chapter III of the land-ceiling law.

predicates.sex_discrimination_challenge_to_land_cei: The proceeding alleges sex discrimination in a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.husband_is_used_as_procedural_representa: The scheme treats a husband as the tenure holder for dealings concerning land owned by his wife.
predicates.wife_ownership_and_compensation_are_pres: The wife retains ownership and is entitled to compensation if her land is taken as surplus.

issues.definition: Treating a husband as a procedural representative is not discriminatory when the wife’s ownership and compensation rights remain intact.

issues.legal_issue: Ongoing consolidation of land holdings does not require ceiling proceedings to abate or prevent the taking of surplus land.
material_facts: Consolidation proceedings were ongoing in some areas while land-ceiling proceedings were also pending.
Consolidation replaced scattered plots with equivalent consolidated plots and provided for compensation and remedies where appropriate.
An explanation to the consolidation law excluded ceiling proceedings from the proceedings treated as abating, and the consolidation law provided for equivalent valuation of replacement plots.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that ceiling proceedings neither abated nor were barred from taking surplus land while consolidation was underway.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 read with Section 5(2) of the consolidation law did not bar ceiling proceedings. The Court relied on the statutory explanation excluding ceiling proceedings from abatement, approved Khetarpal Singh v. State of U.P., and distinguished Agricultural & Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. State of U.P.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding_during_consolidation: A land-ceiling proceeding is pending while consolidation proceedings are underway.
predicates.consolidation_replaces_land_with_equival: The consolidation process substitutes equivalent plots for a holder’s scattered plots.
predicates.ceiling_proceedings_are_excluded_from_ge: The applicable consolidation scheme excludes ceiling proceedings from the proceedings that abate.

issues.definition: Ceiling proceedings continue during consolidation when equivalent plots are substituted and those proceedings are excluded from abatement.

issues.legal_issue: Staggered commencement dates for provisions are not arbitrary merely because they differ, where the dates have rational grounds and the challenge does not establish fanciful selection.
material_facts: The challengers alleged that provisions of the land-ceiling law were brought into force on different dates arbitrarily, contrary to Article 14.

The Court found that some dates were related to preceding legislative steps or an announced policy, and recognized that the State may have multiple relevant considerations when choosing commencement dates.
The Court observed that a challenge brought years later cannot assume that differing commencement dates were capricious merely because the reasons may be difficult to reconstruct.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the temporal-arbitrariness challenge and held that the differing commencement dates did not invalidate the law on the facts presented.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not forbid all variation in commencement dates. The State has latitude to select dates, but neither the legislature nor its delegate may choose fanciful dates; the State should provide a reasoned explanation when dates are challenged.

predicates.article_14_challenge_to_commencement_dat: The proceeding alleges unequal or arbitrary treatment because legal provisions commenced at different times.
predicates.provisions_commenced_at_different_times: Different provisions of the same law took effect at different times.
predicates.dates_have_rational_policy_or_legislativ: The differing dates are connected to rational policy considerations or legislative steps rather than fanciful selection.

issues.definition: Different commencement dates are not arbitrary when challenged under equality guarantees if they have a rational policy or legislative basis.
